articles.title: Partisan bias in a sorted party system: A problem of epistemic inequality
articles.abstract: Normative and empirical scholars typically treat partisans’ distrust of their political rivals as a product of individual cognitive biases. But even if bias is inevitable, it is parties’ coalition‐building and messaging strategies that determine who bias is directed toward. This paper argues that the social sorting of party conflict exacerbates the epistemic and democratic harm of partisan distrust by generating distinctive patterns of epistemic inequality. I show that when voters associate parties with particular social groups, members of those groups suffer greater risk of testimonial injustice and related credibility deficits owing to their perceived partisanship. These dynamics are most damaging for members of marginalized groups, as party–group overlap can reinforce the prejudices they already face. Addressing these harms, I argue, requires looking beyond individual partisans to the background features of party systems that shape how elites mobilize group identities and animus in the struggle for office.

articles.title: Populism, radicalism, and protest mobilization by parties in Europe
articles.abstract: As European democracies struggle with a ‘crisis of representation’, populist parties appear to be instrumental in channeling popular discontent with governments across the continent, including through protests. While contemporary theories propose a strong connection between populism and protest mobilization, this has seldom been tested in a comparative perspective. At the same time, research has found that radical parties are more likely to mobilize for protests, and those parties are often also populist. We empirically disentangle these relationships with a comprehensive dataset of 4.8 million Facebook posts by all active sitting MPs in all EU27 national parliaments plus the UK between 2018 and 2023, using large language models to identify protest-related posts and those that announce protest events. Findings show that it is particularly radical parties mobilizing their followers, with populism itself having little additional explanatory power. This is the first cross-national, longitudinal evaluation of a much-touted theoretical connection between populist parties and protest mobilization, finding that it appears smaller and more conditional than prior research proposed.

articles.title: When opposition leaders speak: personalisation and question time in Australia
articles.authors: Daniel Casey, Thiago N. Silva, Pandanus Petter
articles.abstract: Question Time is a highly visible and adversarial parliamentary arena central to executive accountability, yet increasing personalisation may redirect scrutiny from collective party actors to individual leaders. This article analyses personalisation in Australian Question Time using more than 21,500 opposition questions asked between 1981 and 2025. We examine two dimensions of centralised personalisation: who asks opposition questions and whom those questions target, theorising variation through party structure (single-party vs coalition opposition) and institutional reforms to leadership selection rules. The findings challenge claims of a uniform rise in elite behavioural personalisation. While opposition questioning has become increasingly Prime Minister-centred over time, who asks questions follows a distinct pattern. Leader dominance varies across parties and institutional periods, rising in single-party oppositions but remaining lower and declining in coalitions, and falling further after leadership reforms. These results show that parliamentary personalisation is multi-dimensional and contingent on party organisation and institutional rules.

Different baselines, different outcomes: Reassessing the representative promise of within-party sortition
articles.abstract: Cowley, Webb and Bale’s critique of within-party sortition argues that lotteries among party members cannot produce a socially representative UK Parliament because party memberships are unrepresentative. Drawing on Party Members Project data, they show that random selection would produce only mixed improvements in descriptive representation. While their empirical contribution is significant, this article argues that the broader sceptical conclusion rests on a narrow modelling baseline. Cowley et al. effectively test only one institutional configuration—unstratified random selection from static party memberships—while extrapolating broader claims about sortition as a reform. This article develops three lines of critique. First, their simulations treat party membership as exogenous and unaffected by institutional change, ignoring evidence that candidate selection rules shape recruitment and participation. Second, their analysis evaluates only a single design variant, despite evidence that modern lottery-based institutions employ stratification and corrective mechanisms. Third, their evaluation relies on implicit ‘mirror of society’ standards without specifying formal metrics for aggregating representational trade-offs. Drawing on scholarship on sortition, deliberative democracy, and party organisation, the article proposes a dynamic and design-sensitive framework for evaluating within-party lotteries. Once alternative institutional baselines are considered, the representational potential of within-party sortition appears considerably less constrained than Cowley et al.’s analysis suggests.

articles.title: Not‐so‐great expectations: Outgroup indifference facilitates conflict resolution in negatively interdependent contexts
articles.authors: Smadar Cohen‐Chen, Garrett L. Brady, Gerben A. van Kleef, Eran Halperin
articles.abstract: We examined how responses to outgroup indifference in conflict are shaped by the perceived nature of interdependence, which changes expectations of outgroup emotions toward the ingroup. Unlike conflicts perceived as positively interdependent, we hypothesized that in conflicts perceived as negatively interdependent, outgroup indifference would constitute a positive expectancy violation, thereby inviting favorable responses. Moreover, we examined affective and inferential processes as mediators across four studies ( N = 2521). In Study 1, outgroup indifference (vs. anger and hatred but not hope) reduced negative emotions (but did not affect expected collaboration), subsequently increasing support for cooperation. Study 2 added qualitative measures and showed that outgroup indifference (vs. anger) increased support for cooperation through decreased negative emotions and increased expected collaboration. Study 3 provided correlational evidence that perceptions of interdependence predict participants' expectations of outgroup emotions. Lastly, in Study 4, outgroup indifference increased expected collaboration and emotions when interdependence was perceived as negative.

articles.title: Does disability trump family background? Determinants of electoral participation among young individuals with intellectual disability
articles.authors: Björn Boman, Jonas Hultin Rosenberg, Johan Wejryd
articles.abstract: Systematic differences of electoral participation between various social groups indicate crucial constraints of comprehensive democratic inclusion. Yet, there is a dearth of research on electoral participation among individuals with intellectual disability (ID), whose participation rates are considerably lower than among non‐ID citizens. This study examines determinants of electoral participation among individuals with ID based on administrative records covering five cohorts of individuals from the Swedish upper‐secondary school for pupils with ID ( N = 8438), and their parents. Our main results indicate that the severity of the disability and parents who have voted are the strongest predictors of voting among individuals with ID. The latter suggests that family background is vital. However, the socioeconomic status of the families, such as parents' level of education, income, and occupation, are less pivotal factors.

articles.title: Law enforcement with rent dissipation
articles.authors: Murat C. Mungan, J. Shahar Dillbary
articles.abstract: We consider a framework which brings together losses arising from rent-dissipation and the workhorse model of law enforcement. Governmental actors engage in a contest to share the proceeds from the enforcement of the law through monetary fines, which leads to rent-dissipation. This causes monetary sanctions to be costly, rendering the model used for studying nonmonetary sanctions a better fit for their analysis. The effect of rent-dissipation on optimal sanctions is directly related to the sanction elasticity of offenses measured at the classic optimum (i.e., where the expected sanction equals the direct harm from the offense). When offenses are inelastic, the optimal sanction is smaller than the classic optimum and it is decreasing in the degree of rent-dissipation; and a legislator who does not fully internalize contest costs chooses an overly punitive sanction which is smaller than the classic optimum. The opposite results are obtained when offenses are elastic. We discuss implications and extensions.

articles.title: The political economy of exit protection
articles.abstract: Existing theories explain how exit disciplines governments but generally treat citizens’ ability to relocate as an institutional primitive. This paper instead endogenizes exit protection by modeling jurisdictions that first choose whether to preserve or eliminate mobility before competing through extraction. Although preserving exit uniquely maximizes investment and social welfare, it is not self-enforcing because jurisdictions can profit by creating captive populations. Exit protection is therefore institutionally fragile. The paper then evaluates alternative constitutional architectures capable of addressing this incentive problem and develops one formally. The analysis identifies a benchmark constitutional architecture under which decentralized political orders could, in principle, sustain exit without relying on hierarchical enforcement, repeated interaction, or citizen coercive power.

articles.title: Beyond six versus twelve: Kian v. Florida and the design of the criminal jury
A hangover like any other: the cost of ruling for populist parties
articles.abstract: Populist parties have grown rapidly in popularity in many European countries and have increasingly become common in government coalitions. Because these parties often make expansive promises and derive much of their appeal from their outsider status, entering government may become an electoral liability by the next election. Analyzing populist and mainstream parties in 32 European countries from 1980 to 2023, we estimate the average electoral effect of government participation. We find a post-power penalty of about 4.5–5 percentage points on average. This penalty is remarkably similar for populist and mainstream parties, suggesting that populist parties do not suffer an additional electoral cost from governing. Moreover, the size of the post-power penalty does not vary systematically with growth, inequality, social spending, globalization, or unemployment during the governing term. These findings suggest that bringing populist parties into government does not, by itself, impose a distinctive electoral cost on them relative to other incumbent parties.

articles.title: Gary D. Libecap, Where’s Coase? The implications of economic property rights or rent-seeking in forming institutions
Logrolling affects the relative performance of majority and unanimity rule
articles.abstract: We consider a committee facing binary decisions on a number of proposals. If members vote sincerely and payoffs are symmetrically distributed, we show analytically that simple majority rule is the best q-majority rule in an aggregate or expected payoff sense. We argue that this (well known) pattern changes systematically if the committee faces multiple decisions and members engage in logrolling deals. In a simulation exercise, we find that unanimity rule outperforms majority rule when the number of proposals considered is large enough. We complement our analysis with a laboratory experiment designed to investigate whether human subjects engage in the logrolling deals assumed in our simulations. We find that deals associated with large negative externalities are less likely to arise than others, as are “complex” deals involving many voters or proposals. These results suggest that the impact of logrolling on the relative performance of the decision rules considered may be mitigated by cognitive constraints and other-regarding preferences.

articles.title: Electoral cycles and consumption in India
Constitutional drafting processes and constitutional success
articles.authors: Adam Chilton, Murat Mungan, Mila Versteeg
articles.abstract: Several recent constitution-making processes have been celebrated for being participatory, inclusive, and representative. However, many of these processes also failed. We theorize that aspects of these kinds of constitutional drafting processes could reduce the probability of constitutional success. To show why, we construct a “Constitution Drafting game” (CD game) in which representatives from different interest groups must draft a constitution. We consider the case where the probability of constitutional success is single peaked, but the value from successful adoption is increasing in the degree of issue protection chosen. The drafting process then leads to protection choices that are above those which maximize the odds of constitutional success. Moreover, when the CD game is equivalent to a “nice aggregative game”, as in Acemoglu and Jensen (2013), the maximum and minimum equilibrium probabilities of constitutional success are decreasing in the number of representatives. Within a more specific game structure, we show that the symmetric equilibrium degree of protection chosen by each representative is decreasing in the number of interest groups represented, while the total degree of protection is increasing in it, leading to lower probabilities of constitutional success. We explain how optimism can exacerbate the degree of protection chosen by each party.

articles.title: Gubernatorial partisanship and housing outcomes: evidence from close elections
Social learning behind closed doors: evidence from seniority voting in the US Supreme Court
articles.abstract: We analyze the implications of seniority voting on Supreme Court decision-making. We provide reduced-form evidence consistent with justices learning from the votes of their senior colleagues as determined by the voting mechanism. To explain this evidence, we develop and estimate a model of sequential voting with social learning. In the model, justices weigh spatial payoffs against the appropriateness of their disposition and consider their preferences, private information and the choices of senior justices. We recover estimates of judicial preferences, expertise and learning and use them to assess the quality of Supreme Court dispositions relative to alternative voting mechanisms. We find that the quality of the Court’s dispositions would have improved under an anti-seniority rule, in which junior justices are allowed to vote first.

articles.title: Checks, Balances, and Presidential Ambitions
articles.authors: Christian Fong, Kenneth Lowande, Ayse Eldes
articles.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between running for president and members’ contributions to the core legislative functions that impact Congress’s standing relative to the presidency. This study finds some evidence that ambitious legislators attend roll call votes and oversight hearings at lower rates, but at the same time, they are more legislatively productive, conduct just as much informal oversight and are equally informational in their public oversight. When Congress votes on an issue that affects the balance of power between Congress and the president, they are more likely to side with Congress than legislators without presidential ambitions are. These behavioral differences persist even after their presidential runs, which suggests they are not driven by a strategic effort to audition for the presidency.
